yes, a very bad idea.  You'll be terribly slow because you have not developed any technique whatsoever.  Every new note will look like something entirely new. most people want just that:  begin by some popular "song" they really like, but most probably even the easiest of these will be far beyond your beginner reach.  Playing piano is not such torture. You first must get yourself acquainted with the keyboard and developing a sense of your surroundings and evenness of tempo by playing scales with both hands - a basic scale should suffice for real beginner.  True beginner pieces focus on the area around middle C and then progressively turn to left hand on lower clef and right hand on higher clef. you could use this from a well-known nineteenth century piano pedagogue as a guide: a standard beginner exercise book be sure to play the very first pieces hands separate and then together when you got the rhythm right.  Also note that in these very first exercises both right and left hands are playing in the higher clef in different areas: left hand beginning in middle C and right hand one octave above. This work quickly steeps up in difficulty by around the middle exercises.  You could slow down a bit by trying also the excellent: a collection of finger exercises This pedagogue is not stupid repetitive warm up:  most pieces are short miniatures in early classical style.  He is usually only hated by advanced pianists required to learn his tough technical exercises, but the beginner stuff is pretty sweet.  He was a pupil of a famous composer and teacher of another famous composer. cheers

that's the videogame approach.  I think it might help as much as youtube videos up to some level. most people find it hard traditional notation.  It is not.  It is quite easier knowing which notes to play from notation than from watching a video of someone playing.  "Oh, what was the key that he played again?  *goes back to watch again*".  In the staff they're pristine clear.  The hard part is not *reading* the notes, it is playing them.  YT videos may help reproducing the exact same movements some piano player did, but by merely mimicking it'll not become clear why they did so.  That is the domain of technique and you can never learn that by watching, but by doing.  You discover them yourself as you play didatic material...
